blocks.prompt: 8. The D.C.Os of 11 districts meet to discuss the law-and-order situation in their districts. In how many ways can they be seated at a round table, when two particular D.C.Os insist on sitting together?
blocks.explanation:
11 people at a round table, but two of them must sit side by side.
Plan: tie the two together as one unit, seat the units in a circle, then let the two swap places inside their unit.
steps:
Given: 11 D.C.Os, round table; two particular D.C.Os must sit together.
To find: the number of seatings.
Method: Treat the pair as one unit: \(11 - 2 + 1 = 10\) units in a circle, \((10 - 1)!\) ways. The pair can sit in \(2!\) orders. Multiply.

Count the units
\[9 \text{ others} + 1 \text{ pair} = 10 \text{ units}\]
Why: Gluing the two together makes sure they are always side by side.

Seat the 10 units round the table
\[(10 - 1)! = 9! = 362880\]
Why: A circular arrangement of 10 units (Case-I, a meeting table).

Arrange the pair inside its unit
\[2! = 2\]
Why: The two can sit as (P, Q) or (Q, P); these are different seatings.

Multiply
\[9! \times 2! = 362880 \times 2 = 725760\]
Why: Fundamental Principle of Counting.

Check
\[\text{all seatings} = 10! = 3628800\]
\[\dfrac{725760}{3628800} = \dfrac{1}{5}\]
Why: Without the condition there are \(10!\) seatings. A given person has 2 neighbours out of 10 others, so the chance that P sits next to Q is \(2/10 = 1/5\). It matches.
